items.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001
items.q: Jack formed a band with myself and Alex Foster... And we toured for a while as a band and made a couple of records for Manfred — Manfred, I say Manfred — ECM.

ctx.x: Would you be able to put a percentage of what you play now and attribute any of it to your quote formal education?

Yeah I think so. I don’t know if I’d attribute it as much to the actual education that I got from specific teachers. I think it was more just the experience of being in school playing and developing and being around teachers and other students. And if anything I would attribute certain things of course to, there were a couple of teachers that were very important to me, Herb Pomeroy was one, he was a wonderful trumpet player but his main job at Berklee was to teach — he taught arranging, he taught advanced…

which were small ensembles of anywhere from like four to maybe six people. It could be a couple of horns for the rhythm section — I was in one that was just guitar and saxophone, piano, bass and drums. And it was wonderful because I had to function like a horn player. And I couldn’t read worth — I was terrible. I mean most guitar players will acknowledge that they, it’s a difficult instrument to read on. So I remember when they would first write tunes on the board and the saxophone player could read quite well.…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think my first band had John Abercrombie… I had been working with a group with John and Mick Goodrick

ctx.x: Even though you had a four record deal?

Yeah. We did one more record, and actually there was an instrumental that I wrote called “Festival” that CBS wanted to push as a single, but again we had no money to go out and tour. So at that point I said “Okay I’m gonna go sink or swim with jazz.” They let us out of the contract, and I went back to deciding to be a bandleader and I think

my first band had John Abercrombie… I had been working with a group with John and Mick Goodrick; master guitarist and educator who teaches at Berklee. I had the two guitars and a bassist named Clint Houston. So I called on John. John had been working with Chico Hamilton, and so John played spacy guitar and could go a lot of places I wanted to go. (He) had a sense of humor. So, I think that first bass player was named Peter Warren at the time. I was looking for a saxophone player and I think that Alex Foster was…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: Chick — he told Anthony Braxton, John Abercrombie, Colin Wolcott. So you know that’s where the contribution is — a contribution of giving like a free concert to raise money for CMS.

ctx.x: No. Okay. This is a misnomer then.

Yeah, no. She, you know we helped him you know when they were having some financial problems, Lydia and I — or Lydia arranged and shall we say fundraised the concert. And a lot of prominent musicians came to play there you know — Chick — he told Anthony Braxton, John Abercrombie, Colin Wolcott. So you know that’s where the contribution is — a contribution of giving like a free concert to raise money for CMS. But we were never on a board or anything like that. CMS had their own people doing that, managing the place.

What effect do you think your piano skills have on your approach to drumming, or perhaps vice versa. There’s been a number of drummers who play piano and you’re the most prominent one I can think of, and I wonder how those two things work together, if they effect one another?
